rationale: Both describe altar construction associated with bronze: Chronicles has a bronze altar, while Exodus prescribes a wooden altar with bronze covering on its horns. Chronicles gives twenty by twenty by ten cubits and Exodus five by five by three; the constructions and dimensions remain distinct.

Both describe features encircling the Sea. Chronicles calls them likenesses of calves beneath it and describes their casting in two groups; Kings calls them supports beneath the brim and gives a different formulation of their spacing.

Both connect the completed house with the ark containing the Lord's covenant. Chronicles says Solomon placed the ark there; Kings says he made a place for it and recalls the fathers' exodus from Egypt.

Both describe heaven shut without rain because of sin, followed by prayer toward this place and turning from sin under God's humbling. Chronicles says praise Thy name, while Kings says acknowledge Thy name.
Both anticipate universal human sin and envisage divine judgment handing Israel to captors who deport them to a land far or near.

In both scenes the people witness divine fire and fall on their faces. Chronicles describes descending fire and glory upon the house; Leviticus explicitly describes the offering being consumed. Chronicles also records stone pavement and praise of enduring mercy.

Both describe Solomon and a great Israelite assembly keeping the feast for seven days, with the assembly's extent marked by a named entrance and an Egyptian watercourse. The place spellings and torrent-versus-river wording remain distinct.
Both describe Solomon's chariot cities, horsemen or cavalry cities, and building undertakings in Jerusalem and across his realm. Their additional named places differ and are not made interchangeable.

Chronicles sends Solomon to a coastal location before the voyage in 8:18; Kings locates his work on a ship at a coast. The texts name Gasion-gaber/Ailath in Idumean land and Ezion-geber/Elath in Edom respectively. These are compared as maritime preparation contexts without independently proving the geographic name equations.

Both describe a queen testing Solomon with riddles and arriving in Jerusalem with camels, spices, abundant gold, and precious stones to discuss all in her heart or soul. Her royal designation is queen of Saba here and queen of Sheba in Kings.

Both give four thousand mares for chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. Chronicles says he stationed them in the chariot cities and Jerusalem; Kings specifies the mares as those placed there. The counted objects and the placement wording remain distinct.
